items.body: Passed Recordings thus signs one of its most mature operations: a collective, contemplative, rigorous work, capable of transforming C3 into a small sonic homeland, fragile and vast, familiar and remote, where time bends slowly and sound returns to being a form of attention. Order loses its command, the sequence becomes a constellation 130.81 by Passed Recordings   130.81 chooses the compilation form as an instrument of thought. The initial idea carries as much weight as the sound itself: it guides the hands of the artists, opens a shared field, and invites listening to perform a gesture that has become increasingly rare: to pause within a single note, to let it grow, to watch it change colour, density, temperature. Passed Recordings, a collective born online and later gathered around a concrete practice of sharing, seems to rediscover here one of the most beautiful vocations of ambient culture: building community through attention. C3, with its 130.81 Hz, becomes rule, centre, compass and magnetic field. Each participant enters into relation with that nucleus and bends it toward their own sensitivity, with discretion, patience and artisanal care. The most successful aspect of such a tightly bound project is its mobile quality. The album invites shuffle play, and that possibility genuinely changes the perception of the work. Order loses its command, the sequence becomes a constellation, the pieces call to one another through subtle resonances. In this choice one senses an almost twentieth-century trust in open form, a trust that runs through Eno, certain post-industrial drifts, the long shadow of Basinski, the abrasive matter of Tim Hecker, the slow waters of Loscil, the emotional gravity of Rafael Anton Irisarri, all the way to that lyrical composure Ryuichi Sakamoto was able to entrust to silence. Passed Recordings takes that heritage and carries it into a shared laboratory, with the humility of those who know that a small sound, when observed for long enough, contains an entire climate. “Transforming C3 into a small sonic homeland.” ~Mirco Salvadori 130.81 lives on micro-variations, on harmonic fields that open like luminous dust, on low frequencies breathing with a slow pace, on digital glimmers left to flow toward their natural dissolution. The presence of C acts like a taut thread beneath the surface. At times it emerges clearly, as a mother note, almost a distant organ or a string left vibrating. Elsewhere it becomes specter, grain, electroacoustic tremor, the memory of a tonality recognized more by the body than by the ear. The result possesses a strange intimacy: to listen means following the way thirty-one authors choose the same initial matter and transform it into an emotional landscape, each with their own pace, their own light, their own share of darkness. Small impulses recalling domestic objects filtered through sleep :: The compilation rises above the demonstrative catalog and finds a unified breath. The gentler presences seem to move through a milky half-light, with brushed chords, synthesizer vapors, small impulses recalling domestic objects filtered through sleep. The darker ones widen the mass, searching for deep pressures, mineral drones, dense reverberations, noises that seem to rise from machines left running in a deserted place. The more melodic tracks open essential lines, almost private songs reduced to a filament, while the more abstract ones lead the project toward an area of pure magnetism, where timbre replaces theme and duration becomes thought. Its beauty comes precisely from this fluid alternation: the album preserves its loyalty to the harmonic pivot while allowing different characters to circulate, from drone to ambient music, from post-rock sensitivity to a faint noise-inflected unease, from rarefied miniature to long cosmic immersion. The cover image, that worn yellow crossed by dark marks and a blue shadow, works as a visual index of the sound. There is a surface wounded by time, a matter that has taken in rain, light, oxidation, and continues to emanate presence. The images in the booklet amplify this idea through a sequence of natural, animal, cosmic and domestic visions: veiled seas, starry skies, rocks, snow, a cat, a bird, luminous forms. The graphic project gives the album the quality of a sensitive archive, almost a sentimental atlas built around a note. Each page suggests that C3 can become water, feather, nebula, fur, screen, path, synthetic flesh, low wind. The music confirms that promise and translates it into listening. Within this flow, certain names mark poles of attraction in the continuity of the overall course. Ed Herbers opens a clear and suspended zone, Legacy Systems brings a more extended tension, Jenn Jacobsen introduces a gathered warmth, Unruly Disturbance works on an almost ceremonial idea of C major. Akinetic, with Cryocoma, delivers one of the project’s most physical moments: a vibrant frost, a deep pulse around the tonal centre, harmonics that seem to refract through white matter, a slowness suggesting active immobility. G!GA LURGH tilts the gaze toward wider orbits, Exit Chamber gives the compilation a tone of deep shadow and control, Asha Patera lengthens the breath into an open song, Trees Can Talk ideally closes the graphic and sonic circle with a luminous lament. These are internal signposts within the journey, notes of orientation, small recognisable stars in a broad vault. 130.81 asks for duration, repetition, return, mental disposition :: The value of the album grows when one understands that the limitation chosen by Passed Recordings also concerns an ethics of listening. In an age that pushes every work toward rapid identification, 130.81 asks for duration, repetition, return, mental disposition. It invites us to hear the smallest differences, to distinguish the color of a reverberation, the weight of a sonic tail, the way a low frequency can support a celestial line, the way silence between two musical events creates expectation. The compilation speaks to those who know the history of ambient as an art of permanence and variation, to those who have loved music born at the margins of rock, electronic research and drone, to those who still seek in sound a form of patient listening, almost monastic, with gathered measure and concentration. There is also a human element that matters. The choice to donate part of the sales to Médecins Sans Frontières places the work within a line of solidarity already present in the label’s path. Passed Recordings has often used the compilation as a form of encounter and support, and here that practice gains further grace. Thirty-one artists, one note, a changing listening experience, a concrete destination. The romanticism of musical community, so often invoked and so rarely realised with such coherence, takes form here with measure. Music does what it does best when left to its own dignity: it brings distant sensibilities into relation, gathers minute energies, transforms limitation into shared language. 130.81 is an album to be heard at medium-low volume, letting the low end enter the floor and the harmonics settle in the air. It works through headphones, where every grain becomes an intimate detail, and it works in the open space of a home system, where the central note seems to find new reflections. Its strength is born from the patience with which it cultivates the minimal gesture. Its depth is born from the capacity to make change appear within what seems motionless. In the end, the sensation is that of having crossed a long tide tuned to a single point, a tide in which each wave carries a different signature and each signature agrees to serve a common voice. Passed Recordings thus signs one of its most mature operations: a collective, contemplative, rigorous work, capable of transforming C3 into a small sonic homeland, fragile and vast, familiar and remote, where time bends slowly and sound returns to being a form of attention. 130.81 is available on Passed Recordings. [Bandcamp] 130.81 by Passed Recordings

items.body: The sounds here are not just the contemporary musique concrète we’ve all come to know and love from Everyday Dust, but musique métaphysique. It’s earthy, its rooted, its physical powerful when blaring through the headphones or speakers and subwoofer, but it contains the ever necessary particles of dust that transport me to the otherworld every time I listen to music from this artist. Cavernous sound sculptures Assemblance X Sessions by Everyday Dust   One of the most famous lines in T.S. Eliot’s The Wasteland, comes from The Burial of the Dead section when he wrote, “I will show you fear in a handful of dust.” On Assemblance X Sessions, the ever mysterious Everyday Dust, gives us an earful of fear. Originally transmitted from the depths of the Hollow Earth, these cavernous sound sculptures trace the movement of batwings out from the underworld at twilight to the insect feasting grounds in forests just as dark as the mammoth caves. Perhaps it is better to say these pieces were constructed to celebrate the birthday broadcast of Hollow Earth Art on January 17th, 2026. Hollow Earth Art is a Low Power FM station operating on 104.9 Mhz as KHUH in Seattle, and also streams online. Remember radio? I always like to point out that radio was the original “streaming music” option for music and talk, both on terrestrial broadcasts, and later down from satellite orbits. When the internet came around it was radio stations who pioneered streaming music online. The non-profit community stations like KHUH and many others around the world often have great schedules of music to tune into, with dedicated DJs who have been music fans for years and years and decades and decades. Tapping into the human side of streaming music through seeking out creative radio stations is one of the best ways to get turned on to new artists, hear innovative and eclectic mixes, and otherwise avoid Spotify and other services who are so shitty to musicians. As with their fellow radio non-profits, KHUH, Hollow Earth Radio, “presents a forum for underrepresented music, sounds and perspectives. We support the local music community in Seattle, King County, Washington state, and the larger Pacific Northwest. Our focus is on found sound, field recordings, forgotten music, local musicians, bedroom recordings, low-fi demos, dreams, storytelling, and things that feel real. We expose works that have yet to be unearthed or have long been dormant. We acknowledge and celebrate raw talent and imperfections, and encourage bands who’ve never had their music air on a radio before to take a chance with us.” Musique métaphysique :: DJ Bleek hosts the Urban Mutant show on KHUH and commissioned this work from Everyday Dust. As such it is a delectable entry into the canon of electronic music made specifically for radio broadcast. These are the transmission arts that keep the airwaves interesting. When so much of the radio spectrum has been bought up by corporate interests, it is a truly great thing when the portions of it that remain to world citizens are used for artwork, or in the case of amateur or ham radio, to communicate with one another. Sound art is another case of communication. It communicates something completely different than main radio stream. These streams course up from underground rivers found in those underworld depths. Melded from limestone, calcium and other mineral ore, these reverberant electroacoustic structures are kind of like chamber pieces, if you consider the chamber something you have to reach by moving a way a rock near the roots of an ancient tree and follow those roots through the moist loam until it gives way a labyrinth of branching tunnels and ancient rooms of rock. The sounds here are not just the contemporary musique concrète we’ve all come to know and love from Everyday Dust, but musique métaphysique. It’s earthy, its rooted, its physical powerful when blaring through the headphones or speakers and subwoofer, but it contains the ever necessary particles of dust that transport me to the otherworld every time I listen to music from this artist. There is a touch of foreboding in these sessions, the fear I mentioned at the beginning of this review, but the propulsive journey helps the listener transcend such fear and gain new experiences. This album may be listed as a curio in the Dustopian Frequencies catalog, but is an essential curiosity. Get one for your cabinet. Assemblance X Sessions is available on Dustopian Frequencies. [Bandcamp] Assemblance X Sessions by Everyday Dust

items.body: Necessary Unfold draws together the collective consciousness of contemporary Greek electronic music in their Various Artist label launch collection Part Time Archivists / Part Time Forgers. Coalescing electro, breaks, acid sensibilities, and IDM intent, we get 12 sublime Saturday-night anthems primed for a proper underground, word-of-mouth gathering. Summer radiates through the set. Summer radiates through the set Part Time Archivists | Part Time Forgers by ΠΕΡΑ ΣΤΑ ΟΡΗ   Necessary Unfold draws together the collective consciousness of contemporary Greek electronic music in their Various Artist label launch collection Part Time Archivists / Part Time Forgers. Coalescing electro, breaks, acid sensibilities, and IDM intent, we get 12 sublime Saturday-night anthems primed for a proper underground, word-of-mouth gathering. Summer radiates through the set. We open with Rhythm Code Inc’s electro-break beauty “Corridor,” bouncing across every bar with an instinctive pull toward movement. The hips are locked in early; melodic fugues shimmer above a firm, grounding low-end kick. Mouh Aleb Ish’s “Flashback Recovery” is frankly stunning—snare stutters rattle like gunfire before collapsing into an amen break reworked with imagination, pushing beyond so-called rave tropes into something genuinely revitalized. Magical, and restless. Future Draft keeps the funk tight and taut with “Cutting Edge,” channelling Reece bass pressure and moody tonal shifts, offset by wicked bleep-and-clonk toplines and sweeping, almost cinematic strings. ΠΕΡΑ ΣΤΑ ΟΡΗ drops tek-bass riddims over pole-bent subs and elastic woobs—pure kinetic release, a track that thrives on tension and snapback. TDK’s archetypal breakbeat assault pushes further into rave memory, all 1992 hardcore sensibilities—303 squelch, rapid-fire breaks, and unmistakable Atari-era rawness. Letting bass pressure swell and release in waves :: LEGACY goes straight for acid breaks with a cut that wouldn’t feel out of place on Hard Hands—think “Dark Globe” lineage, but retooled for now. Varonos leans into acid electro with towering synth work, letting bass pressure swell and release in waves before we find a moment of fragile calm in tsev’s “Phone Call from Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Minb [sic],” where piano refrains loop in soft portamento, cycling like memory fragments that won’t settle. DJDim brings machine-funk precision with “TH1S1 5MY7R 4CKD3 3P4C1 D1825,” [I know, right?!] locking the groove into something both mechanical and warm, its acid lines bubbling with a quiet insistence. XU’s “Late Movie” is a tech-funk stepper—confident, strutting, almost theatrical in its phrasing, ululating through polished sonic contours. DJ Tsoug drops a fast, final break-driven piece that resists slipping into drum & bass cliché, keeping things agile and sharp. Closer Athens Computer Underground draws the compilation inward—depth, weight, and a surprising tenderness. Rather than delivering a clean sense of closure, it suspends the energy in a kind of afterglow, where everything that came before seems to refract and settle into something quieter but no less present. It lingers like residual signal, humming just beneath the surface long after the system powers down. Part Time Archivists | Part Time Forgers is available on Necessary Unfold. [Bandcamp] Part Time Archivists | Part Time Forgers by V/A

items.body: Latest Onset Audio release, BMA & Robbyt deliver Arbitrary Arbitrage / Lockbox, a taut two-tracker driven by dark breaks, dense pressure, and full-spectrum low-end hostility. Precision while maintaining a raw, unstable energy Latest Onset Audio release, BMA & Robbyt deliver Arbitrary Arbitrage / Lockbox, a taut two-tracker driven by dark breaks, dense pressure, and full-spectrum low-end hostility. “Arbitrary Arbitrage” unfolds through a slow-burning architecture of half-time step patterns, submerged atmospherics, and tightening rhythmic suspense before collapsing into a kind of controlled supernova. There’s a palpable emotional charge running beneath the production—frustration channelled directly into movement, using anger not as empty aggression but as a productive force against greed, excess, and the hollow ritual of monetary worship. The track’s tension feels psychological as much as sonic. On the flip, “Lockbox” strips things down into a more direct assault: a tightly drilled roller packed with psychotic breakage, brutal drum edits, and thick, phat bass weight. Functional yet deeply unhinged, it hits with precision while maintaining a raw, unstable energy throughout. Brutal and funky. It has not come to play but be played. Arbitrary Arbitrage / Lockbox is available on Onset Audio. [Bandcamp] Arbitrary Arbitrage / Lockbox by BMA, robbyt

items.body: Eight kilometres outside Essaouira, between the douar of Ghazoua and the surf break at Sidi Kaouki, there is a family house named after a Corsican village in Balagne. That is where HabibiSly filmed his debut single, after discovering Gnawa music and following it to Essaouira. Rabbath is the Paris-born son of the Syrian-French double bassist François Rabbath, trained at the Nadia et Lili Boulanger conservatoire and then taken on the road for twenty-five years across four continents at his father’s side. His own project runs on synths, piano, and talkbox, absorbing the Levantine modes of his upbringing through the club nights of Paris’s 18th arrondissement. “Dar Algajola” is the first single from his debut EP Habibi Rhapsody, due in September on Heavenly Sweetness, directed and produced as a video by Athys de Galzain on location in Essaouira, where he records with Saad Tiouly, a young Casablanca maâlem, guembri player and Gnawa singer who has spent years working inside the tradition before pushing it outward into folk, rock and Mediterranean territory, and Aziz Atmani, a Moroccan gnaoui who blends traditional North African sounds with electronic and ambient music. The guembri’s three-string bass drone and the iron clatter of the krakebs sit inside Rabbath’s synthesiser beds, the Gnawa call-and-response riding over programmed percussion, the talkbox bending between Arabic and club frequencies. Gnawa ceremony is built to keep going until the room changes state. This track is built the same way. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — I was pleasantly surprised by this Adrian Belew album, where he blends several of his various facets.A13 sounds very spontaneous; the presence of the piano reminded me of the warmth of Mr. Music Head. Belew plays all the instruments here, and that guitar, which sometimes sounds like the 60s and other times avant-garde, sometimes like King Crimson and other times like the Beatles, Elevator is a return to his song-like format, but played... well played, including virtuosic instrumental parts with a certain degree of risk.A Car I Can Talk To incorporates 50s rock and soul into the blues, with those train station sounds from his extensive repertoire, as vast as a magician's hat.In Backwards and Upside Down, he makes use of his high and low vocals, as well as his most pyrotechnic, 80s-style Crimson guitar, which, almost as if traveling the world, not just time, takes us to Japan.When Adrian Belew picks up a guitar, he can be just as devastating as with an electric one... he has already demonstrated this and does it again in The Power of the Natural World, but with variations compared to the past, with small, almost ethnic instrumental details. In Elevator, he has dressed his guitar in different outfits; it is the undisputed protagonist, along with his voice. Good Morning Sun finds novel discoveries in the editing and layering of instruments.The Saturday Morning Roar revisits the experiments with electronic music, where the backing tracks, along with his guitar improvising synthesized solos, reach one of the album's greatest peaks. When only the piano remains, it takes on a different meaning. Many colors...many facets...many sounds...many overlapping layers make up a fun Belew.Attitude interweaves keyboard arrangements with intricate guitar scales that allow for layering.Taking My Shoes Out for a Walk features more textures...acoustic guitars and spoken word over aggressive sections reminiscent of the Henry Rollins Band.At times, it sounds like Allan Holdsworth, a style that continues in Back to Love, the album's final and most experimental section, in this almost chronological journey through influences, including volumes one, two, and three from the first decade of the 2000s.A whole sonic framework that, remaining in Fripp's band, wouldn't have allowed him to develop, and yet we find those sentimental fragments that were in King Crimson (which we know were his) in Beauty, and an ending with Seventy Going on Seventeen that reminds me a lot of early Bowie...which is very special coming from Belew...I could almost hear him singing it, and the album is completed as a synthesis that contributes meaning but with joyful passion.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Conceived during the tour for the previous album, Led Zeppelin's second volume is so distinct that it possesses its own autonomy. The approach is more direct, the sound is rawer, the songs seem tailor-made for live performance, and Page's growth as a riff-maker, one of his many facets, encompassing hard rock, blues, and soul, is gradually evident. However, certain litanies, remnants of psychedelia, can detract somewhat from the effectiveness, diverting the focus, as can be seen in "Whole Lotta Love" or "Moby Dick." These disruptions might be justifiable in a live performance, but in the studio version, they diminished the impact of gems that otherwise would have shone even brighter. Beyond this compositional observation, the band was at the height of its creative powers, brimming with ideas, and each member contributing their own unique touch.What Is and What Should Never Be breaks new ground, with jazzy undertones and a fusion of 60s British pop, blues, and funk... all within a song format, with Jimmy Page knowing when to glide peacefully and when to attack with deadly ferocity.Throughout Volume II, John Paul Jones's presence grows enormously, underpinning the foundations of the tracks until he becomes indispensable. Robert Plant had already developed his own style, making his voice another instrument and another flagship of the quartet's sound.The Lemon Song continues as a fundamental building block in what is constructed on this second album, where if it teaches us one lesson, it's that the blues is always something more, a vehicle to add elements and enrich the journey. And John Paul Jones's bass, which one can hear at times in addition to Jimmy's guitar, and the groove achieved were limitless.Led Zeppelin was always more than just good music. Unlike other bands on their contemporaries with similar characteristics, a certain mystical air gradually awakened within them, particularly in Jimmy Page, and that aura was transferred to compositions like "Thank You," music by Page and lyrics by Plant, an instant classic, almost like entering a chapel with muddy boots...guided by John Paul Jones' organ, before returning to the plea in "Heartbreaker," and another immortal guitar riff (not many can say the same). And fundamentally, there was that communion of the group, whose chemistry was at its best, those years when they were like an indivisible unit...recording together, traveling together, eating together, and that translated into the music.With "Living Loving Maid (She's Just A Woman)," they do whatever they want with time and rhythm, constantly changing them, making the song another example of instantaneous change within a song format, stretching and forever altering it. "Ramble On" will be a first approach to that electro-acoustic format that they will fully explore in Volume III, with Plant dressed in one of his many guises, and again the bass roving alongside the guitar, driving the rhythm of the composition. A funky, groovy drum rhythm that becomes Andean-like with guitars on the cliffs, with Page already playing his intricate parts that nevertheless seem simply enchanting in their placidity. And therein lies its charm!They could explode...and they could curl up in a corner...Bring It On Home closes a bluesy album full of contrasts, trying out different outfits and sharpening their weapons for the future...everything was here waiting for the moment to be used...but masters of the stage...lighting only what they wanted to be seen...the quintessence of a band that covered ground with an aerial perspective.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — The Basque culture that straddles the northeastern part of Spain and southwestern region of Francehas fascinated linguists and anthropologists alike owing to the fact that this culture appears to beone of the last remnants of Paleolithic Europe before the arrival of the Indo-Europeans. Given thisculture's rather isolate position in terms of its relationship amongst other European cultures, it'slittle wonder that it too has developed some of its own unique musical styles. While little known tothe outside world, the Basque region did indeed participate in the flavorful sounds that emergedduring the psychedelic and progressive years and thanks to DJ Makala who compiled a number of tracksfrom various artists, this excellent compilation is like a box of assorted chocolates awaiting yourdiscovery.KATEBEGIAK Prog-Rock, Psych-Folk & Jazz-Rock Music from the Basque Country was released in 2021 andhighly acclaimed for showcasing some of the region's history that was the crucial link thatconnected the folk revivalists of the 1960s and the Basque Radical Rock (Euskal Herriko rockerradikala) that fueled the regions punk scene. The term KATEBEGIAK actually means "Links of achain." The album features 13 select tracks that display the wide array of experimental sounds thatsprang up in the 1970s and continued into the 80s. After the 60s revival movement, bands began tocross-pollinate their homegrown folk music with the various forms of psychedelia, rock and jazzfusion that were springing up all around Europe and the world since the mid-1960s and this Whitman'ssample pack is the perfect place to dip in and get a taste of such sounds for further exploration.This release features all the expected artists such as the most popular Basque act Itoiz as well asHaizea, Enbor and Errobi but also features some of the rarest of the rare with bands such as thePamplona based Magdalena and the virtually unknown Urria. Strangely this collection features arather interesting choice of what to include and what not as it features the track "Pello Joxepe"which as an outlier from rest and features a Mississippi born black psychedelic soul singer coveringa traditional Basque song and yet the release doesn't include real Basque acts that existed at thetime including Sakre, Akelarre, Mirotz and Patxi Villamor. Track lengths vary considerably as wellranging from the 3 1/2 minute "Agurra II" from Enbor to the longest track "Andere" from Errobi whichsprawls out to 13 1/2 minutes. While these acts varied widely in approach, the thread that keeps it all connected is the softsensual folk and oft flute oriented music that in some ways resembles Celtic folk music but soundsas distinct as the language this unique population has kept alive despite all odds. Some of thetrack placements are a bit odd as the opening "Egunaren Hastapena" by Haizea takes a good fiveminutes to slowly work up to some sort of song structure. The following "Xori Bele" by Izkaitzwould've been a better choice as it provides a more direct introduction into the culturalsmorgasbord about to be experience however this is hardly a deal breaker as all the tracks areworthy of an attentive listen. While most of these artists are clearly more in the psychedelic folk camp with touches of prog rockin for the mix, bands like Lisker actually deliver the more rocking bravado whereas the tracks byAmala Zubrina & Pascual Gaigne along with the album's closer by Urria are extremely ethereal and themost experimental. Despite the urge to play these in a different order it's the music that countsand although i've heard of many of these bands i haven't actually heard them so this is the perfectway to get acquainted as well as finding some rarities that have completely escaped the attention ofeven the most sleuth oriented databases. The Basque scene was quite distinct from the Rock Andaluzand jazz fusion scenes of the rest of Spain and this compilation is the perfect way to explore thisoften neglected region of the nation. Pretty much every track works for me however i wish theexcluded acts were on this one too.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — After delivering a fairly unadulterated slice of traditional Basque folk music on its debut, HAIZEAjoined the late 70s craze of incorporating elements of 70s prog and 60s psychedelia into its mix andin the process took a huge leap with a substantially more adventurous and explorative sophomorerelease. On HONTZ GAUA which is Basque for "Night of the Owl," guitarist / vocalist Txomin Artolaleft the group in pursuit of a solo career and in his place flautist and guitarist Xabier Iriondojoined the ranks and helped usher HAIZEA into much more progressive territories with its set of fivetracks that only added up to just over 33 minutes. A much more avant-garde album, HONTZ GAUA wasbuilt around the same traditional Basque folk melodies of the debut only embellished with moreethereal atmospheric effects, less rigid compositional structures and extended excursions that wereinspired by the European progressive rock of the 1970s.The opening track belies the album's ambitious nature with a rather tame traditional approach."Anderea" sounds like a leftover from the previous album but starting with the second track"Egunaren Hastapena" the band blossoms quite quickly into a darker tone with less predictable songstructures all the while the feminine charm of Amala Zubira takes on a darker at times even gothicapproach sounding something like if Sandy Denny was auditioning for Dead Can Dance. Althoughprimarily acoustic in nature, electric guitars are used more liberally this time around withpsychedelic dressing applied to tracks like "Argizagi Ederra" to great affect as well asincorporating more demanding time signature approaches rather than untempered guitar chordstrumming. Irondo adds a lot of intricate flute moments as well as adding the distinguished tones ofthe Portuguese guitar. "Arnaki" offers a twin guitar effect which takes the music into a 60spsychedelic vibe.Once again all lyrics are in the Basque language which offers a unique rhythmic flow unlike any ofthe Romance languages and therefore sounds quite distinct from the Rock Andaluz acts that wereflooding Spain in the 70s. Touches of jazz are incorporated for musical textures but nothing in thefusion sense ever intrudes on the rather subdued psychedelic light-hearted nature of the album evenwhen the twin electric guitars are at the most feisty. The jewel in the crown is the side long titletrack broken down into two distinct segments which at over 14 minutes offer plenty of excursionsinto true unrestricted progressive territories. Beginning with a Gregorian chant followed by abaptizing water sound effect sequence before gently rolling out the flute and acoustic guitar beforethe ethereal vocal harmonies kick in. Tender percussion is added and the track oozes around quicklyskillfully as it shape shifts through various musical motifs steeped in heavy psychedelic effectswith some sort of chimes and intricate changes through varying passages. Easily the best track ofthe band's career.The light airy feel of the album laced with beautiful melodies and adventurous performances in anexotic language may make you feel like you've drifted away into some far away land as HAIZEAaugments its Basque folk traditions into powerful psychedelic folk statements. Laced withtraditional wind instruments and various percussive techniques, HONTZ GAUA adds a sense of darknessliving up to its title meaning of "Night of the Owl." Zubiria delivers an excellent display of vocalcontrol evolving beyond her cutsie good girl folk style of the debut and the icing on the cake arethe explorative shifts in song structure that feel organically natural and not hastily thrown intothe mix. A guest violinist delivers some serous melancholy and band displayed a remarkable maturityon this sophomore offering most likely due to the fact much time was spent the previous yearsbetween albums on the live circuit and best of all the band seriously integrated the progcharacteristics perfectly. A charming mellow album that is one of the highlights of the Basqueinfused prog folk craze of the era.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — HAIZEA (means "wind" in Basque) is one of the more recognized names when it comes to Spain's late70s progressive folk scene from the Basque region and existed from its formation in Hondarribia in1975 until its demise in 1980. The band released two distinct but vastly different albums duringthat time with this self-titled debut more in sync with the Basque folk revival scene that dominatedthe 1960s while the band's second release "Hontz Gaua" explored more daring experimental excursionsinto the world of electric psychedelic folk with much more complex arrangements. While the bandexperienced quite a few lineup changes during its five year run, amazingly the band's two albumsfeatured mostly the same members including vocalist Amaia Zubiria, guitarist / vocalist Xabier Lasa,bassist Gabriel Barrena and drummer Carlos Busto. This debut would be the only album for guitarist /vocalist Txomin Artola who would be replaced with flautist / guitarist Xabier Iriondo on the band'ssecond album.Prog lovers will probably find little interest in this debut as the band was still very much in thetraditional folk revival stage of the previous decade however with all the Basque musical flavorscorrupted by the experimental commingling of progressive rock and psychedelia imported from abroad,this debut does give a crisp clear glimpse into what the world of unaltered Basque folk actuallysounds like and that would be very similar to a lot of other European folk structures despite theBasque language and culture emerging as an anomaly isolate on a continent long overtaken by Indo-European tribes conquering the Paleolithic cultures. Obvious references on this lead to British folkacts such as The Pentangle or Steeleye Span however Basque folk sounds more similar to Celticflavors from not only Spain but the Breton region of France and of course Ireland, Wales and partsof Scotland. No bagpipes here though!While the second album was a crash course in how to update your traditions in the brave new world,HAIZEA's debut is the polar opposite of keeping things as authentic as possible with gentle folkrock instrumentation, a timeless atmospheric presence with all the tracks heavily rooted in the mosttraditional Basque folk melodies sounding much more like a Smithsonian Folkways release ofhistorical recordings than a so-called modern day progressive band but nonetheless the band performsbeautifully with a light airy feel that finds dual male and female vocals trading off along withgentle acoustic arrangements. While the the instrumentation is almost exclusively acoustic, snippetsof electric guitar do seep in on tracks like "Ura Ixurirk." The most notable different betweenBasque folk music and other European flavors is the strange rhythmic patterns that emerge from theband singing exclusively in Euskera, the native term for the Basque language.While this will not be considered essential for those seeking the more adventurous undertakings ofthe second release, this album is beautifully performed and for lovers of ethnic folk musicalexpressions i can't think of a better place to dive into the little known sounds of Basque folklorethan this debut by HAIZEA. The band's name which means "wind" really does shine though on this debutas the album passes by like a nice gentle breeze near the northern coast where Spain and Francemeet. Although there are few traces of anything progressive or experimental on this one it still isworth exploring simply as a point of reference as to how the Basque folk style was incorporated intothe context of prog rock and psychedelic folk from not only the band's sophomore release but themajority of other bands that were jumping on the progressive bandwagon after the collapse of theFranco dictatorship. The final track "Arrosa Xuriaren Azpian" at ten minutes with psychedelicovertones provides a vital clue to the band's next step. As an ethnic music lover i find this onequite pleasant as music like this is like a time machine that gives a glimpse into the collectivesoul of a culture even though i much prefer the good juicy experimental stuff!

items.body: Review by martindavey87 — Black Sabbath's aptly titled 'Vol. 4' is the British metal pioneers' fourth studio album, and once again, it's another release that I struggle to really get into. I don't dislike Black Sabbath, I enjoy most genres of music and most bands, from any era. But for whatever reason, the stars just do not align because I just don't "get" the first few Black Sabbath albums. I'm sure there's a point, perhaps later in their career, where the band just clicks with me, but their first few records, often revered as metal masterpieces by fans, just do nothing for me. It's not all gloom and doom though (well, it kind of is!), as there are a couple of highlights. 'Snowblind' is a fantastic song, probably ranking up there as one of my Sabbath favourites, cheesy ballad 'Changes' has some great vocal and lyrics, and 'St. Vitus Dance' has some interesting guitar work. But overall, I find the rest of the tracks just seem to plod along, similarly to how I felt about their previous releases. I've tried and tried, and have had this one on my playlist for a while, but it's just not working for me. Perhaps I'll have more luck with their next album?

items.body: Review by martindavey87 — Let's just be honest here, does anyone actually go out of their way to listen to this album? The thing is, it's not bad, it's just, well? weird. 'Time Requiem', a progressive metal band specializing in lightning-fast flurries of notes in a neoclassical vein, is the product of keyboard mastermind Richard Andersson. They'd only released one studio album prior to this, so like? why produce a live album so early in their career?It just seems unusual. I don't know a lot about the band, but I would take a guess that, like other, similar groups, they probably don't gig very often, if ever. And with a limited choice of songs, it just doesn't really offer much for the listener to sink their teeth into. For what it's worth though, the performances are fantastic. Each member of the band plays with machine-like precision. The sound is very good, and the crowd seem quite receptive to the band, though my guess is that this isn't typically a Time Requiem audience. It could also just be that I've always preferred studio albums to their live counterparts. But overall, this isn't a bad release, but I doubt I'll ever listen to it again. I'll just stick to the bands studio output instead.

items.body: Review by TenYearsAfter — Ruud Dielen had a long history with cover bands , playing guitar in songs from Jimi Hendrix, Santana, Led Zeppelin, Queen, Toto and Genesis. After many years touring in the more commercial circuit, he decided that it was time to write his own music and in 2017 he produced his first album entitled Aquarius, as a one-man-band (guitar, bass and synthesizers), under the name Glorious Wolf. The music sounds as a tribute to the Seventies era progrock and Classic Rock, from Pink Floyd to Zappa and Hendrix, embellished with a wonderful array of vintage sounds (from Moog, Mellotron and Hammond to Gibson, Fender and Mesa Boogie). On his second album Zodiac (2019) and third Mysterious Traveller (2023) Ruud started to invite male and female singers, and to blend the progrock sound with a more song-oriented and varied musical attitude. On Prog Archives Ruud Dielen his Glorious Wolf project got a lot of praise for that musical formula, meandering tastefully and elaborately between instrumental Old School vintage keyboard drenched progrock and song-oriented tracks. And now, anno 2026, here's Ruud again (playing acoustic - and electric guitars, fretless bass, Precision bass, synthesizers, mellotron and FX drums) with Glorious Wolf, featuring a range of national and international guest musicians, on vocals, drums, bass, Hammond, Yamaha piano, Mellotron, theremin and saxophone. Most of the foreign musicians Ruud had met during an international musical collaboration.Elements of Hope Pt.1 ? Instrumental (4.34) : This new album starts with an exciting electronic music atmosphere featuring pulsating sequencers and spacey synthesizers, then howling and biting Gilmourian guitar runs, topped with Mellotron choirs, followed by a tight and catchy beat. The music is embellished with Ruud his powerful guitar runs, fat synthesizer flights and soaring Mellotron choirs, and backed by a fluent rhythm-section (Kike Paglia on drums and Tim Ros on bass). In the end majectic Mellotron choirs erupt, wow, what an impressive start!Elements of Hope Pt.2 - Carrying this Yoke (6.15) : The intro delivers psychedelic sounding Mellotron violins. The music turns into a folky climate with acoustic guitar and fragile English male vocals (by Frank van der Borg), in a slow rhythm. Gradually a more lush sound featuring Mellotron violins, and powerful vocals and guitar riffs. In the final part a break with raw guitar riffs and propulsive drum beats. Lots of contrast, variety and dynamics, and tastefully arranged.Elements of Hope Pt.3 - Into the Clouds (5.55) : First celestial female vocals (by Jyoti Verhoeff) and twanging acoustic guitar, in a dreamy and hypnotizing climate, wonderful. Now the sound becomes more lush, embellished with fretless bass, slow drumbeats and distinctive female vocals. Gradually the atmosphere is working to a symptuous climax with a synthesizer solo, powerful drums and Hammond, culminating into fiery guitar solo, how exciting.Elements of Hope Pt.4 ? Instrumental (1.42) : A short piece in an ominous climate, with raw and powerful guitar, and slow and powerful drumbeats, the interplay is awesome.Elements of Hope Pt.5 - Life's Chaotic Spell (5.51) : The final part of this 5-pieve epic title track contains omnipresent Hammond, blended with exciting rock guitar, powerful male English vocals and a propulsive rhythm-section. Now saxophone play (by Reg Parham) joins, strongly coloring the music, with hints from Frank Zappa and King Crimson. Finally a heavy guitar solo, backed by a dynamic rhythm-section and Hammond.If You Please ? instrumental (6.20) : This composition delivers a slow rhythm and a compelling climate, Ruud really shines with his guitarwork, from sensitive to fiery, and using the tremolo-arm and wah-wah pedal, prog meets bluesrock, wow. Halfway beeps and bleeps, then a more atmospheric sound featuring spectacular wah-wah driven guitar runs, backed by propulsive drumbeats.If I Only (5.46) : After an intro with Mellotron (by the late Thomas Zunk) and militairy drums the music turns into a slow rhythm with heavy guitar, strong male vocals and gradually a more bombastic atmosphere. Halfway a fiery guitar solo, with howling and biting leads and Hammond layers, the music builds and builds, very compelling and exciting.Whirlwinds & Maelstroms ? instrumental (6.44) : Another Mellotron soaken intro, then slow drumbeats and powerful guitar. Halfway a swirling Hammond solo (XK5 Hammond with Leslie by Harry Knapen), followed by a heavy guitar solo, the interplay is excellent.Everything Must Break to Grow - EoH Pt.2 Reprise (6.25) : The final track on this new album starts with dreamy piano and vocals, then a slow rhythm, in a melancholical atmosphere, topped with subtle slide guitar. Gradually the sound turns into more lush and powerful featuring rock guitar and a dynamic rhythm-section. Finally dreamy with spacey synthesizers, guitar and voices, another example of Ruud his interesting and varied musical ideas.In the 3 years after his previous effort Ruud has moved and built a high-tec studio in his new home. You can hear the result: a mature and elaborate new album on which the music is wonderfully meandering between Old School prog and a more varied and song-oriented musical approach, embellished with his awesome guitarwork, vintage keyboards and vocal leads, and backed by good musicians. After Edo Spanninga (as E.D.O.) with his solo album The Past Is A Foreign Country, his other project Trion with Terra Tiempo here is another excellent new Dutch prog effort, well done Ruud!

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Empath' is undoubtedly one of the most eclectic and unbridled albums Devin Townsend has everrecorded. Conceived as some sort of magnum opus, this 2019 release encompasses a diverse range ofmusical influences from the Canadian musician's extensive back catalogue - everything from blastingavant-garde metal and progressive rock to symphonic music, ambient, and dance-pop (well, the lastone is a bit ironic, but you get the picture) is part of this ambitious and maximalist progexcursion. A huge, bold, and resonant work of art, 'Empath' is to my understanding a celebration ofthe musical universe of Devin Townsend, with all of its quirky, corny, overblown and elementalfacets. Joined by co-produced Mike Keneally, this record features a rather impressive set of guestmusicians and contributors, too, including the likes of Adam "Nolly" Getgood of Periphery who isresponsible for engineering and mixing the album, drummer Morgan �gren of Kaipa who has somesongwriting credits, and Steve Vai, among many others, who contributes a flamboyant guitar solo atthe very end of the album.Made up of ten album tracks, each song on 'Empath' explores a particular corner of the DevinTownsend sound. Opener 'Genesis', with its prelude 'Castaway', is a quirky piece of prog rock withcomplex, wacky arrangements, heavy guitars and a string of surprising sounds, and for many one ofthe most representative Devin pieces on this album. 'Spirits Will Collide' then follows up with abeautifully orchestrated triumphant sound, while the fourth track 'Evermore' marks a return to thedense and heavy sound that we're more familiar with. Stylistically, this song reminisces theuplifting prog metal Townsend had explored on his 2009 album 'Addicted'. We then have the excellent'Sprite', which is one of the more experimental entries on 'Empath', combining seamlessly electronicsynth sounds with winding symphonic music. 'Hear Me' is a manic piece of metal (think of SYL as areference), and unlike the classically-inspired song 'Why?', captures one of the most maximalist DTperformances on this record. The 11-minute-long 'Borderlands', which is the next major highlight, isa really playful piece of energetic prog metal, only followed by the six-part suite 'Singularity',sitting at twenty-three-plus minutes of playtime. Featuring a string of complex shifts and thetypical Wall of sound style of production, this is one of the most powerful and angular epicsrecorded by Townsend, and while parts of it are really impressive, I would hardly call it theperfect epic as it can occasionally feel a bit too hectic and immense.Nevertheless, 'Empath' is a fabulous solo album from Devin Townsend that aims to represent the all-encompassing nature of his music, uniting together on the same record the full range of musicalinfluences that make up his world. Surely one of the impressive and memorable releases of 2019.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The third and final part of Gong's Radio Gnome Invisible trilogy, where Zero, the hero, receives his cosmic ascension, activating his third eye...deserved an imposing musical framework, befitting the importance of the events narrated. This volume thus became the most musically daring, the most experimental, and the one with the longest tracks. While each part was unique in its own way...and Angel's Egg had innovated with the short duration of its tracks and yet all its stylistic variety, You further developed these concepts, taking them a step further and becoming a classic not only for the band but for the genre itself.As the cover promises...there's a mix of spacey atmosphere and indigenous mysticism in Thoughts for Naught, Daevid Allen's composition, his ability to draw the rest into his universe...Tim Blake's synthesizers and Mike Howlett's bass in Magick Mother Invocation, creating that spacey psychedelia that always starts slowly...Didier Malherbe's saxophone, Gilli Smyth's vocals, and of course Pierre and Beno�t Moerlen's drums and percussion...plus Steve Hillage's ineffable and unmistakable guitar...everything will conspire to make that conjunction of stars explode in this volume.Master Builder is the construction of that curtain of synthesizers and the Buddhist choir...the percussion, the flute in an oriental orchestra...until the drums introduce the saxophone and the space rock jam...the cosmic French psychedelic free jazz begins...you can smell the 70s...you can feel it...there is precision, there is technique...yes...but there is also madness, freedom, anarchy, bohemianism, and that mix is ​​what made this Gong so special, ultimately, Allen's invocatory presence. When Hillage begins to play...nobody was prepared for that cascade of sound...for those doors that open in the mind with the notes of his sound...which, supported by the synthesizer, the drums and the bass, will make history.You is an album that wasn't rushed...in a decade that seized control of time to do with it as it saw fit for artistic purposes...and if this meant accelerating it to the point of confusion like King Crimson on Red...or slowing it down to the point of despair...like Gentle Giant on Free Hand...there was no doubt they were going to do it, and Gong took the time to build each step of ascent on You...because they knew that the feeling of climbing step by step is not the same as skipping steps in pursuit of a rush that only speaks of detachment from things.As layers of synthesizers build upon the drums in A Sprinkling of Clouds, and the drums with each hit seem to leap from the speakers and reach us as only a few records can...and the guitar sounds wild yet clean at the same time and you can follow its path at every moment...when Didier Malherbe joins in we understand why they distanced themselves from anyone who could do something similar and Frank Zappa's Inca's Roads didn't end up going in the same direction either.Perfect Mystery revisits the cabaret atmosphere of Angel's Egg only as a connection within the story, that oriental atmosphere that sets the stage for The Isle of Everywhere, one of the album's central themes...where synthesizers, Gilli Smyth's vocals, bass, and drums create an atmosphere reminiscent of King Crimson's Islands...only to then turn around and take another route, because Mike Howlett's swing on the bass had the necessary propulsion to soar without sopranos...and Gong sometimes has the ability to pass the third eye to us, if we can connect with his music; it's jazz...it's progressive rock...it's funk...it's psychedelia...it's the Canterbury scene, born in part because an Australian couldn't return to England and had to stay in France.Steve Hillage's solo begins so subtly behind the saxophone...but it does define itself throughout the entire development, supported by the bass and drums, at times playing with parts of jazz rock, until You Never Blow Your Trip Forever encompasses everything heard so far in the trilogy, even more psychedelic if possible...until it settles as if unintentionally into a section that, from improvised and played, culminates in another inspired song/prayer to the universe...a mantra repeated and destined to fade away, the complete opposite of this third volume of the most classic Gong which, as if it were a loop in time...must be repeated again and again once it has already ended.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As if a metronome were forcing its angle further and further outwards...expanding the range until it distorted...the trio, which didn't evoke the image of a trio, begins its second album with "A Visit to Newport Hospital," showcasing organ variations that sound like alarms, red alerts...Dave Stewart combines the magic of the 60s with the mysterious psychedelia that in the 70s would give way to that other Canterbury metric, and Mont Campbell with his measured vocals, plus the organ overlays from which the guiding threads would emerge, the solos of that melody which, as promised at the beginning, were nothing more than alarms of variation on the same note. Jazz and Bossa Nova are implicitly present...staining like raindrops on petals. The alarm awakens us.Contrasong features two tenor saxophones and two trumpets...the monotonous rhythm goes hand in hand with Mont Campbell's singing, and that piano that cuts through Clive Brooks' drums...which cuts through the trumpets...and cuts through the saxophones...and suddenly we're in uncharted territory...like that cover that looks like molten lead, whose solidifying shapes were once used to predict the future... where the trio that did not evoke the image of a trio preferred the mystery of the promise of what it suggests...but is not seen, what is, but is not yet known...an eternal advance, which postpones its realization with the concrete certainty of something that can be heard...can be felt...but not touched, and that when trying to understand it moves away, and comes closer if the mode of perception changes.Boilk is more variations, but in reverse...another way of confirming that intellectual understanding only sets us back...is by not understanding the proposed rules...which are reminiscent of Gy�rgy Ligeti and works like Atmospheres. When, in the final coda, Stewart's other great passion emerges with the Baroque religious organ.Long Piece No. 3 is the album's centerpiece, and here Bach's counterpoints become progressive, slicing through space until they become silence, and then a floating, sidereal space sustained by the drums. Here the trio plays at being a quartet, with the organ's bass lines, leading to an even more ethereal section with the piano...where, from atonal, they could become aggressive, provocative, but always maintaining the tension, that mystery of not knowing what will come next...what note, what chord awaits around the return of the nebula.The second part continues with the variations, the key to the album, creating spacey atmospheres...where that molten lead seems to solidify and take shape...but new suspended melodies, which distanced them from other bands of the genre, anchor them with that Hammond organ with one foot in the 60s, the same as Pink Floyd's Atom Heart Mother, but firm to the pattern that it is the organ that leads the race, this race without a visible final objective.The third part is considered the most complex, alternating between keyboard and piano, with the piano sections being the most virtuosic and classically accomplished. At times, it recalls the darker segments of Emerson, Lake & Palmer's Pictures at an Exhibition.The fourth and final part is even faster, related to Soft Machine's debut, but the jazzy Bossa rhythm with the keyboard cuts and repetitions, plus the bass and the out-of-tune keyboard, end up distancing it and solidifying this experiment of variations as the triumph of melodic harmony in all its forms.

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — According to ProgArchives, Il Bacio Della Medusa's sophomore album, Discesa Agl'inferi D'un Giovane Amante, is the not only the greatest Rock Progressivo Italiano record of the 21st century, but also one of the greatest progressive rock albums of the 2000s overall (as of writing this, it stands in the top 50 albums between 2000 and 2025). I had incredibly high expectations going into this, because I honestly thought modern rock progressivo italiano couldn't get better than Logos and Unreal City, so I was indeed hoping for a masterpiece. And somehow, it could get better than those. This is hands down the absolute pinnacle of modern Rock Progressivo Italiano and one of the finest pieces in the subgenre. It holds beauty, tragedy, insanity, and power all tied into an imaginative and epic journey. The music found on here is very sophisticated and well crafted, with there being an overwhelming sense of classical influences scattered across the record as the band also pays tribute to the classic Italian bands of the seventies, all with a new twist of horror and stunning visuals the music can put into your mind when listening to it. The entire album consists of 12 individual tracks, but they all function as one continuous composition. The first two tracks, Preludio: Il Trapasso and Confessione D'un Amante, actually have no drums and are more akin to mellow and sometimes even romantic-sounding chamber music, and they do an amazing job at introducing the listener to what music here will sound like and acting as the calm before the storm. From here on out, most of the remaining tracks are just absolutely astounding, and each has a staggering amount of details with incredibly intricate arrangements spliced into every moment. The titles of these pieces are each quite lengthy and depict very vivid pictures about the concept of this record, but in the end the long titles don't bother me when the music here is this good. Numbers like La Bestia Ed Il Delirio, Ricordi Del Supplizio, Nostalgia Pentimento E Rabbia, Sudorazione A Freddo Sotto Il Chiaro Di Luna, and so many other tracks are legitimately some of the strongest Rock Progressivo Italiano I've ever heard, and it's phenomenal the way the band never misses a beat when it comes to keeping the energy and atmosphere going for each one. Each of these and the other ones have everything I could've ever wanted from an Italian album. Raspy vocals, vibrant flutes, intense, unhinged heavy-rocking electric guitars, and even soft and sweet acoustic and classical guitars combined with passionate string work. I really enjoyed how the band balances all the deranged and unpredictable parts with the charmingly quiet yet moody ones. The music is always developing and never stops growing and pushing into different sectors of the story, and it always changes the mood perfectly with the musical direction, and the mind-blowing talent of how these musicians play their instruments throughout the whole is also just the cherry on top for the whole thing. In conclusion, I completely agree with ProgArchives in that this album is truly a remarkable piece of art. Maybe not a completely perfect masterpiece, but definitely a near-perfect masterpiece! Going into this, I knew the album was supposed to be good, but I honestly didn't know it would be THAT good. This is in between a high 4.5/5 and a low 4.75/5 and is a must-listen for any fans of progressive rock, not just of Italian progressive rock. And one more note, this is surprisingly the only Italian album to achieve my "Number 1 album of the year" award, that year being 2008.

items.body: Im Jahr 1969 wurden »die kulturellen Barrieren, die Japans zahlreiche Künstler:innen und Entertainer:innen lange voneinander getrennt hatten, endlich beseitigt«, schrieb Julian Cope 2007 in seinem bisweilen zweifelhaften, aber doch essenziellen Japrocksampler. Das Jahr sei ein Wendepunkt gewesen und habe ein neues Zeitalter der Experimente eingeläutet, dessen Ergebnisse »unglaublich energiegeladene Werke hervorbrachten, von denen sich viele jeder Kategorisierung entzogen«. Far East New Rock Invention 1969–1975, veröffentlicht als Teil der Wamono-Reihe von 180g, dokumentiert die Genese dieser neuen Sounds. Unter den neun Stücken finden sich bekanntere Vertreter wie die Far East Family Band, Yuya Uchida & The Flowers und deren Nachfolger, die Flower Travellin’ Band – hier in Kollaboration mit dem Terumasa Hino Quintett –, größtenteils stammen sie aus dem Katalog von Nippon Columbia. Viele der zugehörigen Alben wurden zuletzt neu aufgelegt. Die Zusammenstellung zielt offensichtlich darauf ab, diese lose Bewegung, die ihre Inspiration aus Hard- und Psych-Rock, Folk und gelegentlich der Avantgarde-Musik bezog, einem breiteren Publikum nahezubringen. Doch auch die Heads können darunter Nuggets entdecken, beispielsweise Cuts des The-Dynamites-Mitglieds Hiroshi Segawa sowie Takeshi Inomata & Sound L.T.D.s rasender Jazz-Fusion-Freak-Out »Black Angel«. Far East New Rock Invention ist die Art von Compilation, die ihr Publikum dazu animieren will, tiefer zu diggen. Das lohnt sich ja.

items.body: Dass von einigen Musikern gilt, dass sie stets mit neuen Ansätzen überraschen, mag selbst so eine Phrase sein. Bei Will Yates alias Memotone stimmt das in dem Punkt, dass er seinen Ansatz tatsächlich von Platte zu Platte verändert oder zumindest verschiebt. Ob das dann noch für Überraschungen taugt oder schon zur erwartbaren Konstante gerät? Was auf Warm Shadows ganz sicher unerwartet kommt, ist der Fortgang von Stück zu Stück. So lässt die Titelnummer am Anfang vermuten, dass Yates seine Klarinette erneut in verschiedenen Zusammenhängen erkundet, mit sich langsam vorantastendem Jazz und einer elektronischen Verfremdung des Blasinstruments, die an eine Verneigung in Richtung Jon Hassell denken lässt. Gleich im nächsten Song, ja, doch, singt dann die litauische Musikerin Ugnė Uma nach einem gesprochenen Monolog über verhaltenen einzelnen Gitarrentönen und einem ostinat im Hintergrund tackernden Rhythmus, der weniger Beat als durch diskretes Zittern tragende Zeitstruktur sein möchte. Der Beat versteckt sich auch in der folgenden Nummer, die man als Improvisieren mit Ambient-Elementen deuten kann, ohne dass klar ist, was für Instrumente da genau zum Einsatz kommen – Streicher? Echte? Konstant bleibt auf der Platte die friedliche Grundstimmung, die zugleich von unaufhörlicher Neugier getrieben scheint. Da kann man zwischendurch schon mal bei einer Indie-Rock-Nummer landen, die derart aufs Knappste arrangiert ist, dass sich beim besten Willen keine Rock-Klischees darin finden. Überraschung. Gute.

items.album: Ivan Pavlov interview: ‘The book is the final Soisong release’
items.excerpt: Ivan Pavlov, who records as CoH, co-founded Soisong with the late Peter “Sleazy” Christopherson in Bangkok in 2007. The project produced the octagonal “Soisong EP” tour CDEP in 2008 and the full-length “xAj3z,” which documented two European tours. The project held its final concert at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010 – without Christopherson, whose health had declined to the point that he could not fly. Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010.
items.body: Ivan Pavlov, who records as CoH, co-founded Soisong with the late Peter “Sleazy” Christopherson in Bangkok in 2007. The project produced the octagonal “Soisong EP” tour CDEP in 2008 and the full-length “xAj3z,” which documented two European tours. The project held its final concert at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010 – without Christopherson, whose health had declined to the point that he could not fly. Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010. A 2012 event at Bar Bonobo in Tokyo, the venue where the project’s first concert had taken place, marked a symbolic close. On May 22, 2026, Pavlov released “Soisong Book” – a 160-page faux-leather hardcover limited to 222 numbered copies – through the official Soisong store. The book draws on email correspondence, private photographs, official announcements, manifestos, and items Pavlov describes as “fake documents”: promotional materials created during the project’s active years. Two CDs are affixed inside the cover: a 2007 Tokyo concert recording pre-dating Soisong’s formation, and a new studio album by trumpet player Julio Ecclesiast, who contributed to “xAj3z.” Side-Line spoke with Pavlov about the archive behind the book, the nature of some of Soisong’s listed performers, the night in Berlin, and what follows this release. Soisong interview SL: The book draws heavily on email exchanges between you and Sleazy. How large was that archive, and what guided your selection process? Were there exchanges you wanted to include but felt were too private? Ivan Pavlov: I have about a thousand emails in my mailbox filed under ‘Sleazy’, but since it’s a Soisong book, only those that relate to the process have been included. SL: You described upscaling late-2000s cellphone photos and low-res Myspace images using current technology. Where did you draw the line between restoring what was there and altering it? Did any images come out looking wrong once upscaled? Ivan Pavlov: Good upscaling algorithms do not alter images to anything one would be able to notice in print, so no, the printed images look the same as their low-res originals. SL: The book includes what you describe as “fake documents.” Can you give a specific example – were these created during the project’s active years, or produced later for the book? Ivan Pavlov: You can see them in the book. For example, as part of the campaign for Soisong album called ‘xAj3z’ we had published a so-called Report from an, obviously non-existent, Investigating Committee. The report speculated on and promoted the shape of the CD package as an extraterrestrial object, with multiple illustrations. This was all made back in 2009. SL: 222 copies is a precise figure. Is there a reason for that specific number, or was it determined by print-run economics? Ivan Pavlov: You may find in the book a rather extensive dialogue about choosing the name for the project. I won’t expand too much on that, but ‘song’ is ‘two’ in Thai language. As for the economics for any kind of small editions – it is tough, indeed. SL: The first CD captures the 2007 Tokyo concert where CoH and The Threshold House Boys Choir performed as separate acts – a pre-Soisong moment. Why that recording specifically? Was it already in the archive, or did it require sourcing? Ivan Pavlov: Back then, a few days after the show I received 2 CDs from the sound engineer who was at the main desk during the concert. One with a room recording, i.e. including the sound of the audience, one with the clean signal. I now made a mix of the two and I see it as a document well related to Soisong – in the book you will find a mention of the show, and the subsequent discussion on playing live. SL: The second CD contains a new studio album by Julio Ecclesiast, the trumpet player from “xAj3z.” How did that collaboration come about – did you approach him, or did the idea come from him? How much input did you have in the direction of his album? Ivan Pavlov: Just like several other participants in Soisong, Julio mostly exists in domains of imagination, listener’s imagination included. Which already back in 2009 had become a rather typical, important part of Soisong’s approach to choosing the performers. SL: Soisong’s packaging choices were consistently unusual – the octagonal CDEP, the warning on “xAj3z” that it could only play in CD players with a flat horizontal tray. How much of that approach came from Sleazy, and how much from you? Ivan Pavlov: I would usually come up with rough geometrical design ideas, which we then perfected through a mutually encouraging dialogue. SL: The final Soisong show took place at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010, without Sleazy. What do you remember about that night, and what was the decision behind going ahead without him? Ivan Pavlov: There was no decision making as such, as far as I remember we were about to play a few shows in Europe, but then Sleazy’s health suddenly declined which didn’t let him fly. The show in Berlin was too late to cancel, so we went on with this kind of ‘remote version’. Sleazy recorded a video message to the audience, and a video stream for me to play during the show. I played the music. It felt quite lonely on the stage, I admit. SL: Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010 – the city where Soisong was based. How did you decide what to do with the project’s archive after that? Was there a point where you considered closing it entirely? Ivan Pavlov: Soisong is pretty much closed ever since Sleazy’s departure. Whatever has been published afterwards – these are just echoes of the past on their way to the future. Soisong was only meant to last until 2012, so in 2012 we organised the symbolic final event at Bar Bonobo, in Tokyo. That’s where Soisong played the very first concert, commonly referred to as Test Run #7. During this final night at Bonobo in 2012, with the help of the bar’s owner Koichi Sei and a few other friends, the recording of Test Run #7 was released in a small edition of sealed Walkman CD players. Some years later, I also managed to put together the unfinished Soisong album ‘kAm1e’. Now comes the book, which is pretty much just a collection of artefacts. I believe we would have published this kind of the final statement if Sleazy was alive, too. SL: Dais Records released a remastered deluxe 2LP of “xAj3z” in 2025, with one previously unreleased track, “Lom Tum Lai Kwee.” How did that reissue come about, and what was it like returning to that material? Ivan Pavlov: Dais expressed interest in re-issuing the two Soisong releases on vinyl. I wouldn’t have been able to pull that off on my own, and the idea seemed attractive. So I agreed and we did it. As for coming back to Soisong material – be it email conversations, images or music – it always feels warm, feels like coming home. SL: You said the book’s creation was fuelled by “the same joyful enthusiasm and sense of fun as every other publication.” How would you describe Soisong’s working method to someone who only knows the music? Ivan Pavlov: Encouraging joyful enthusiasm in each other, and working with a sense of common fun – that is the only method we employed. SL: Does “Soisong Book” function as a closing document, or is there still archive material that could surface in future releases? Ivan Pavlov: The book is the final Soisong release. I might do a few more commemorative fake radio-broadcasts for soisong.bandcamp.com. I would also definitely like to work more with Julio Ecclesiast, which largely depends on how he feels about that… but officially as Soisong, there are no further releases planned. Soisong Broadcast #13 by SOISONG About Soisong Soisong was an experimental electronic music project formed in 2007 by Peter “Sleazy” Christopherson and Ivan Pavlov (CoH), based in Bangkok, Thailand. Christopherson had previously worked with Throbbing Gristle, Psychic TV, Coil, and The Threshold Houseboys Choir, while Pavlov released music under the CoH name. The project combined Pavlov’s computer-based composition with Christopherson’s work on artificial vocals and what the project described as “South Seas” instrumentation. The first release, “Soisong EP,” was an octagonal tour CDEP issued in 2008 in disposable-design packaging, with the release title doubling as a password for additional material on the project’s website. The full-length “xAj3z” followed, in octagonal packaging and carrying a warning that the disc could only play in CD players with a flat horizontal tray. Live activity included the 2008 Test Run Tour – with dates in Tokyo, Rovereto, Copenhagen, Bilbao, Amsterdam, Moscow, and Athens – and a 2009 reunion tour with shows in Linz, Moscow, St. Petersburg, Wroclaw, and Cologne. The final concert took place at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010, performed without Christopherson. Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010. A 2012 event at Bar Bonobo in Tokyo, site of the project’s first concert, served as a symbolic close: the recording of that original Tokyo show, Test Run #7, was issued in a small edition of sealed Walkman CD players. Pavlov subsequently assembled the unfinished album “kAm1e.” Dais Records reissued “xAj3z” as a remastered deluxe 2LP in 2025, with the previously unreleased track “Lom Tum Lai Kwee” added to the Bandcamp edition released on May 30, 2025. “Soisong Book,” released May 22, 2026, is confirmed as the final Soisong release.

items.body: Belgian duo Gare Noir is driven by Sam Claeys and Frits Standaert, both also known for their involvement with Red Zebra. After Red Zebra pressed the pause button, the pair began working on their own material, which first resulted in a series of singles and eventually culminated in the release of their debut album “This Is Gare Noir”, featuring twelve tracks. It quickly becomes clear that both musicians draw heavily from the golden era of the 1980s and the New-Wave movement, yet they manage to inject enough personality and individuality to make the album feel remarkably diverse. Starting from a foundation of New-Wave and Post-Punk, the duo occasionally takes detours into Pop and Rock territory, creating a record that constantly shifts in mood and texture. The entire album is masterfully stitched together, alternating between harder moments and more ethereal passages. Several songs evolve toward genuine climaxes, largely thanks to strong arrangements, clever build-ups, and the sheer power of certain choruses. The charismatic vocals naturally add even more strength and identity to the material. Above all, however, these songs radiate a sense of enjoyment and spontaneity. At times, I can hear traces of Ultravox blended with elements reminiscent of Heaven 17, before the album gradually moves into darker and more distinctive territory. Personally, I would not have minded if the album had leaned even further into darker atmospheres, but it is clear that “This Is Gare Noir” aims for a broader audience rather than confining itself to a specific niche scene. (Rating:8). Listen to “We Spin”: https://wagonmaniac.bandcamp.com/track/we-spin

items.body: We have Vancouver’s own Verboden Festival coming up this weekend in our backyard, and we’re excited about seeing a slew of familiar faves like SRSQ and Male Tears as well as catching acts we’ve been tracking through studio material but have yet to catch live, like Dildox and More Ephemerol. Hope to catch up with regular readers/listeners, too – should be a great weekend. On with this week’s tracks! Scimitar Street Sects, “No Percentage In Caution” The pair of LPs released by long-standing industrial punk terrorists Street Sects gave us a lot to chew on last year, and the band’s declaration that they’re moving in a “more rhythm based/song focused direction” with their new stuff is intriguing. This first sample clearly finds some of the harmonic and synth hook elements of the Full Color Eclipse second being drawn into a rhythmically tight package. No Percentage in Caution by Street Sects Sydney Valette, “I Fucking Love You” We’ve come to associate Sydney Valette with a more continental and very French take on modern darkwave, avoiding many of the cliches of the style in favour of something that feels both classic, but without being beholden to the ur sources of the sound. New single “I Fucking Love You” holds with that, but sounds more strident than any of Valette’s work in recent memory. Partly it’s the tempo and push of the song, but also it’s a distinctly wounded and gothic vocal delivery, bringing out the emotion and drama here. If this is the direction of the new record, it could signal a nice shift into a new direction that would certainly be of interest to us as fans and followers of his work. I Fucking Love You by Sydney Valette Ortrotasce, “As I See It” Ortrotasce always keeps you on your toes; from single to single and within the run-time of the occasional longer release the one-man project deigns to release you’re never exactly sure where in the sprawling fields of synthpop, EBM, darkwave, and new beat things might land. You even have to keep your head on a pivot mid-track, as the peppy, Kraftwerkian programming of this early electro number is swiftly offset by a gloomy and resigned vocal which feels wholly separate. As I See It by Ortrotasce Transmigration, “Understanding” Last we checked in with the UK’s Transmigration, we noted their capacity to make the kind of gritty dark electro that benefits from obscurity and rough edges. New cut “Understanding”, the first taster from EP Living Information isn’t a huge leap away from that aesthetic, but it’s also a lot sharper and more direct, with atmosphere evolving out of the vocals, the speedy sequences and the aggression of the delivery, almost as a byproduct. The result is one of urgency, with a lot of the power stemming from how open and direct it all is, creating a sound that doesn’t need to be dressed up at all, arriving unforced, unadorned and hard-hitting. Living Information by Transmigration Scimitar, “Zenith (Inhalt remix)” Little bit of a ID:UD twofer this week with this Scimitar remix by Inhalt. We’ll be seeing the Los Angeles based band for the first time at Verboden this coming weekend, and we’re quite keen to do so; as an act we’ve tracked for a few years, they’ve consistently put out material that defies a lot of dark alt music trends, capturing sounds that are spiky, punky and uncompromising. And (spoilers) this week’s episode of We Have a Technical has Matia Simnovich of Inhalt as a guest, talking about the art of being a producer and what that entails. Tune into the latter, and then next week to hear our impressions of the performance from the former! Zenith (Inhalt Remix) by Scimitar Nikonn feat. MeLLLo, “Lighthouse” Lastly, something fairly off-format for us but still salient to our coverage. MeLLLo, AKA Marianthi Melitsi of the on-hiatus but never far from our playlists synthpop act Marsheaux, makes a guest vocal appearance on the new single by London producer Nikonn, and her familiar, soothing tone glides perfectly over this downtempo mix of dreampop and chillout instrumentation, making us wistful for the sorts of crepuscular ballads which complemented Marsheaux’s club numbers so very nicely. Lighthouse by Nikonn feat. Melllo The post Tracks: May 25th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.
